questions.question: A 26-year-old female with a bleeding disorder following autosomal dominant inheritance. She gave the history of her father and sister having the same bleeding disorders. What is the most likely disorder?

explanation.text: Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder caused by defective or deficient von Willebrand factor (vWF). It follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, affecting both males and females, with a 50% chance of passing the disorder to offspring.

Von Willebrand disease is clinically and molecularly heterogeneous, with three identified types, each exhibiting a variety of phenotypes. vWD type 1 vWD Type 2 vWD Type 3 Autosomal dominant. The most common type. Mild to moderate vWF deficiency. Quantitative defect. Point substitutions prevent the vWF protein from maturing or cause it to leave the plasma quickly. Autosomal dominant. Qualitative defect.

Types: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N 2A ( Most common ) - Decrease in binding between vWF and Gp1b/9 Missense mutations cause faulty multimer formation → the most active forms of vWF, i.e. large- and intermediate-sized multimers are absent. 2B - Increase in binding between vWF and Gp1b/9 2M - VWF-dependent platelet adhesion is decreased. VWF binding to platelets is impaired.

Type 2M VWD typically has mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding 2N - There is a marked decline in the binding affinity for factor VIII. The level of factor VIII is lower when compared to the VWF: Ag. This led to misdiagnosis as haemophilia A. Autosomal recessive. Quantitative defect.

Produced by frameshift mutations or deletions affecting both alleles (autosomal recessive), which produce little or no vWF. Factor VIII levels are also lowered because vWF stabilizes factor VIII in the blood, and the resulting bleeding condition is severe.

**Hemophilia A (Option B):** is an X-linked recessive disorder that mainly affects males, with females being carriers. This makes it an unlikely diagnosis for this patient, who has a family history involving females.

**Christmas disease (Option C):** is an X-linked recessive disorder; hence, this condition is primarily seen in males, and it is less likely to be the cause of an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
**Factor X deficiency (Option D):** is a rare bleeding disorder that can be inherited in autosomal recessive patterns, which causes the clotting process to take longer than normal.

questions.question: A young patient presents with a large retroperitoneal haemorrhage and a history of intermittent knee swelling during strenuous exercise. There is no history of mucosal bleeding. Which of the following deficiencies is responsible for the condition mentioned above?

explanation.text: The patient's symptoms (large retroperitoneal haemorrhage and knee swelling) suggest haemophilia, which is typically caused by deficiencies in Factors VIII (Hemophilia A) or IX (Hemophilia B). This condition is characterised by spontaneous or trauma-induced joint and muscle bleeds but not mucosal bleeding, which is distinct from von Willebrand disease or platelet dysfunction.

Aspect Hemophilia A Hemophilia B Deficient factor Factor 8 deficiency Factor 9 deficiency Pathway affected Intrinsic pathway defect APTT Elevated BT, PT, and TT Normal Treatment Cryoprecipitate, Recombinant factor 8 (Humate) Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) Hemophilia C is due to factor 11 deficiency, an autosomal recessive condition. Bleeding episodes are generally milder than in Hemophilia A and B.

**Incorrect Options: GP1b/IX (Option B):** This is associated with Bernard-Soulier syndrome, a platelet disorder characterised by defective platelet adhesion. It leads to mucosal bleeding, which is absent in this case. Von Willebrand factor (Option C) deficiency causes von Willebrand disease, which primarily results in mucosal bleeding (e.g., nosebleeds, gum bleeding) and not typically large retroperitoneal haemorrhages or joint bleeds.

**Lupus anticoagulant (Option D):** This is associated with antiphospholipid syndrome, leading to an increased risk of thrombosis (clots), not bleeding. It does not explain the bleeding symptoms described in this patient.

questions.question: Which of the following shows maximum amplitude on thromboelastography?

explanation.text: Thromboelastography (TEG) measures the viscoelastic properties of blood as it clots. The maximum amplitude (MA) on TEG reflects the strength of the clot, which is primarily determined by the number and function of platelets and the fibrinogen concentration. The platelets contribute most significantly to the clot's strength and the MA value.

Thromboelastography (TEG) is a diagnostic tool used to evaluate coagulation profiles and guide management with transfusions and hemostatic therapies. Studies show that TEG can reduce blood product usage by up to 40%, decrease postoperative length of stay, and lower the risk of reoperation. TEG measures the viscoelastic properties of blood as clotting occurs.

The resulting data is plotted on a graph with time on the x-axis and amplitude (clot strength) on the y-axis. Key values include: Reaction time (R): The time it takes for the clot strength to reach an amplitude of 2 mm. Kinetics (K): The time from R to when the amplitude reaches 20 mm. α-angle: The angle formed by a line from R to the point where K intersects with the 20 mm amplitude mark. Maximum amplitude (MA): The highest amplitude reached.

Lysis at 30 minutes (Ly30): The per cent decrease in amplitude 30 minutes after MA (or 60 minutes in some cases). Inference: A prolonged R time may indicate coagulation factor deficiency or anticoagulation. A decreased α-angle can result from hypofibrinogenemia Low MA can be due to thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Increased Ly30 indicates hyperfibrinolysis, often seen in severe trauma or with thrombolytic therapy.

Based on the TEG findings, targeted blood products can be administered to normalize coagulation. For example: Fresh frozen plasma for prolonged R time Cryoprecipitate for decreased α-angle Platelets for decreased MA Tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid for increased Ly30.

questions.question: Below is an image of the coagulation cascade activation following closed endothelial injury. Identify the factor ‘L’, which combines with tissue factor to activate factor IX.

explanation.text: Factor VII (Proconvertin) combines with tissue factor to activate factor IX in the Coagulation Cascade following closed endothelial injury. When tissue factor is exposed due to endothelial injury, it forms a complex with Factor VII. This complex activates Factor IX by cleaving it to Factor IXa, which then participates in the coagulation cascade.

**Factor XII (Hageman factor) (Option A):** is involved in the initiation of the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. It is not directly responsible for activating factor IX in response to closed endothelial injury.

**Factor VIII (antihemophilic factor A) (Option C):** plays a crucial role in the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade. However, it is not involved in the direct activation of factor IX in response to closed endothelial injury. vWF (von Willebrand factor) (Option D) is a glycoprotein that plays a vital role in platelet adhesion and aggregation. It is not directly involved in activating factor IX in the coagulation cascade following closed endothelial injury.

questions.question: Leiden mutation is of factor:

explanation.text: The Leiden mutation is a genetic alteration in Factor V, a protein essential for blood clotting. It has the autosomal dominant type of inheritance. The mutation makes factor V resistant to inactivation by protein C, disrupting an antithrombotic pathway and increasing the risk of thrombosis.

**Factor VIII (Option B):** plays a key role in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation, where it activates Factor X to Xa, which then helps in the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, leading to the formation of a blood clot. It is not associated with the Leiden mutation.

**Factor I (Option C):** , also known as fibrinogen, is the precursor to fibrin, which forms the structural framework of a blood clot. When bleeding occurs, fibrinogen is converted to fibrin by the enzyme thrombin during the final steps of the coagulation cascade. It is not associated with the Leiden mutation.

**Factor X (Option D):** , also known as the Stuart-Prower factor, is a key enzyme in the blood clotting process. It is activated to Factor Xa and plays a crucial role in converting prothrombin to thrombin, ultimately leading to the formation of a blood clot. It is not associated with the Leiden mutation.

questions.question: Which of the following clotting factor deficiencies will not affect clotting in vivo?

explanation.text: Factor XII deficiency (Hageman factor) does not significantly affect clotting in vivo, as it primarily participates in the intrinsic pathway and is involved in the activation of the fibrinolytic system and the contact activation of the clotting cascade. Factor XII does not notably impair normal clotting, as other factors and pathways can compensate for its lack.
In contrast, Factor VII, Factor V, and Factor IX deficiencies significantly impact the clotting cascade and lead to bleeding disorders.

**Factor VII (Option A):** is a critical component of the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. Deficiency can lead to bleeding disorders, as it directly impacts the initiation of the clotting cascade in vivo.

**Factor V (Option B):** is essential for the common pathway of coagulation, acting as a cofactor for Factor Xa in the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin. Its deficiency results in impaired clotting and increases the risk of bleeding.
**Factor IX (Option D):** is involved in the intrinsic pathway of coagulation. Deficiency causes Hemophilia B, leading to impaired clot formation and increased bleeding risk in vivo.

questions.question: Which test evaluates the extrinsic pathway?

explanation.text: Prothrombin time (PT) evaluates the extrinsic pathway of coagulation. It measures the time it takes for blood to clot in response to activating agents that initiate the extrinsic pathway, primarily involving factors VII, X, V, II (prothrombin), and fibrinogen.
Incorrect Options: Option A - aPTT: Activated partial thromboplastin time evaluates the intrinsic pathway of coagulation.

Option C - TT: Thrombin time measures the time it takes for fibrinogen to be converted into fibrin by the action of thrombin. It evaluates the final common pathway of coagulation and is used to assess the activity of thrombin.

Option D - Bleeding Time: Bleeding time assesses the primary hemostasis, specifically the ability of platelets to form a platelet plug and initiate clot formation. It measures the time it takes for bleeding to stop after a standardized skin incision.

questions.question: A CKD patient had to undergo dialysis, and his Hb was 5.2 g/dL. So two blood transfusions were to be given. The first bag was completed in 2 hours. The second was started, and in the midway, he developed shortness of breath and hypertension. Vitals were BP: 180/120 mmHg and pulse rate: 110/min. What is the cause?

explanation.text: Transfusion-related circulatory overload (TACO) occurs when a patient receives blood or fluid too quickly. In the given case, the patient undergoing dialysis received two blood transfusions. overwhelming the cardiovascular system's capacity to handle the increased volume. Symptoms of TACO include shortness of breath, hypertension, elevated blood pressure, and fluid overload.
Incorrect options: Option A: Allergic reaction: While allergic reactions can occur during transfusions, they typically present with symptoms such as itching, rash, hives, or anaphylaxis.

Option C: Transfusion-related acute lung injury: TRALI is a rare but potentially serious complication of blood transfusion characterized by acute respiratory distress and pulmonary edema. While shortness of breath is a symptom of TRALI, hypertension and elevated blood pressure are not typically associated with this condition.

Option D: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction: A febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction is characterized by fever and chills during or after a blood transfusion, usually due to antibodies in the recipient's blood reacting to donor leukocytes.

questions.question: A patient who receives recurrent transfusions for thalassemia develops fever and chills during this time. There is no evidence of hemolysis. Which of the following measures can decrease the rate of transfusion reactions?

explanation.text: The patient's presentation with fever and chills with no evidence of hemolysis is suggestive of a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction. Leukoreduced red blood cells (RBCs) refer to blood products that have undergone a process to remove or reduce the number of leukocytes. White blood cells can trigger immune responses and cause transfusion reactions, including febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions.
Leukoreduced RBCs reduce the risk of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions. Incorrect options: Options B, C, and D do not reduce the risk of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions.

explanation.text: The coagulation cascade involves a series of sequential activation and interactions of various clotting factors, leading to the formation of a stable fibrin clot.
Incorrect Options: Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: Which of the following is the major source of plasma Von Willebrand factor?

explanation.text: Endothelial cells, which line the blood vessels, are the primary source of plasma von Willebrand factor. These cells synthesize and release vWF into the bloodstream. Von Willebrand factor produced by endothelial cells plays a crucial role in blood clotting and platelet adhesion to damaged blood vessel walls.
Incorrect Options: Options A, B, and C are incorrect.

questions.question: Acid mucin is stained by:

explanation.text: Alcian blue staining is specifically used to detect and visualize acidic mucopolysaccharides, such as acid mucin. It is often employed to identify mucin-producing cells, mucous glands, and mucin-rich connective tissues. Alcian blue staining results in a blue or bluish-green color, indicating the presence of acid mucin.

Incorrect options: Option A: PAS: PAS staining is used to detect and highlight the presence of carbohydrates, including glycogen and mucopolysaccharides. It is commonly used to stain structures such as basement membranes, glycogen granules, and fungal organisms. PAS staining results in a pink-to-magenta coloration.

Option C: Masson trichrome: Masson trichrome staining is a staining technique used to differentiate various tissue components. It involves staining collagen fibers blue, cytoplasm and muscle fibers red, and nuclei dark red to black. While Masson trichrome staining can help visualize connective tissues and collagen, it does not specifically target acid mucin.

Option D: Phosphotungstic acid haematoxylin (PTAH): PTAH staining is commonly used to highlight muscle fibers and fibrin. It is particularly useful in diagnosing muscle disorders and identifying abnormalities in muscle structure.

questions.question: What does the following image show?

explanation.text: Emperipolesisis a cellular process in which one cell is engulfed and contained within the cytoplasm of another cell without being degraded. It is a non-destructive process, unlike phagocytosis or autophagy, where the engulfed material is typically broken down and degraded. Incorrect options: Option A: Autophagy: Autophagy is a cellular process that involves the degradation and recycling of cellular components.

It is a mechanism by which cells remove damaged organelles, misfolded proteins, and other cytoplasmic constituents. Autophagy plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis and responding to various stress conditions.

Option C: Phagocytosis: Phagocytosis is a process by which cells, such as macrophages and neutrophils, engulf and internalize solid particles, such as bacteria, cellular debris, or foreign substances. The engulfed material is then enclosed within a membrane-bound vesicle called a phagosome, which fuses with lysosomes for degradation and destruction of the engulfed material.

Option D: Amoebic autophagy: Amoebic autophagy refers to the autophagic process observed in amoebae, which are single-celled organisms. It involves the engulfment and degradation of cellular components or particles by the amoebae to obtain nutrients or eliminate unwanted materials.

questions.question: What is the color of the vacutainer that contains sodium fluoride?

explanation.text: Sodium fluoride is used as an additive in vacutainers to prevent glycolysis in blood samples. The vacutainer tube that contains sodium fluoride as an additive typically has a grey color. The grey-top vacutainer is specifically designed for glucose and lactate determinations, as sodium fluoride acts as a glycolysis inhibitor.
Incorrect Options: Options A, C, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: Prolonged bleeding time is seen in:

explanation.text: Prolonged bleeding time is seen in Von Willebrand disease. Von Willebrand disease is a bleeding disorder caused by a deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (VWF), a protein involved in platelet adhesion and blood clotting.
Incorrect Options: Options A, B, and D: Prolonged bleeding time is not seen.

questions.question: What is the maximum duration for TRALI to occur after a blood transfusion?

explanation.text: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is a potentially severe complication that can occur after a blood transfusion. It is characterized by the sudden onset of respiratory distress and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema. TRALI typically manifests within 6 hours after a blood transfusion. Incorrect options: Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

questions.question: A 32-year-old male requires a blood transfusion after a severe bike accident. He is known to have the Bombay phenotype. Before the transfusion, his blood sample is sent to the laboratory for compatibility testing. Based on his blood group, which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: Lack of H, A and B antigens on RBCs
options.B: Lack of H, A and B substances in saliva
options.C: Lack of antigens of several blood group systems
options.D: H, A and B antibodies will always be present in the serum

explanation.text: People with the Bombay phenotype (the rarest blood group in the world) express no A, B, or H antigens on the red blood cells. (Option A ruled out) They are homozygous for the silent h allele (represented as h).

The antigens are not present in the saliva, either. (Option B ruled out) As the antigens are not expressed, the serum will always present the H, A, and B antibodies. (Option D ruled out) Antigens from other blood group systems (e.g., Rh, MNS, etc.) are still present on the RBC (Option C) It is strongly associated with leukocyte adhesion defect 2 ABO antigens are present not only in the red blood cells but also in the other blood cells, in most body fluids (except CSF), cell membranes of tissues such as the intestine, urothelium and vascular endothelium.
They do not lack antigens from other blood group systems.

questions.question: A 23-year-old individual is scheduled to donate blood for a local blood drive. To ensure the safety of the blood supply, the donor's blood will be screened for various infectious diseases. Among the following options, which one is typically not included in the routine screening for donated blood?

explanation.text: Dengue fever is a viral illness transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Unlike some other diseases listed, routine screening for dengue in donated blood is not typically performed. This is because mosquitoes primarily transmit dengue rather than through blood transfusions. Screening for transfusion-transmitted infections: The following infections can be transmitted by blood transfusion. Viral Bacterial Parasites Others Hepatitis (A, B, C, G).

HIV (I & II). HTLV (I & II). CMV. EBV. Parvovirus B19. Syphilis Malaria Babesiosis Trypanosoma cruzi Creutzfeldt- Jakob disease Plasma processing methods have been shown to inactivate most recognised infectious organisms, except for non-lipid-enveloped viruses and prions. All clinically relevant blood components transmit prion disease following a single blood transfusion.

Malaria can also be transmitted by most blood components (red cells, platelets, white-cell concentrates, cryoprecipitates, and frozen red cells after thawing and washing). Transmission from single-donor FFP has not been reported. In India, the following five diseases are screened: HBV (Option B). HCV. HIV (Option C).
**Malaria (Option A):** . Syphilis. Screening for the diseases mentioned above is mandatory, and transfusing unscreened blood is a medical offence.

questions.question: Which of the following can be used to store blood for up to 42 days?

explanation.text: Blood can be stored for up to 42 days in SAGM Additive solutions used for storage of blood products: Anticoagulant Full form Shelf Life ACD (Option A) Acid citrate dextrose 21 days CPD (Option B) Citrate phosphate dextrose 21 days CPDA (Option C) Citrate phosphate dextrose adenine 35 days SAGM (Option D) Saline-adenine-glucose-mannitol 42 days SAGM also contains CPD as an anticoagulant.

Actions of ingredients of additive/anticoagulant solution: Glucose: ATP generation by glycolysis. Adenine: ATP synthesis & increases the shelf-life of RBC to 35-42 days. Citrate: Prevents coagulation by chelating calcium. Sodium-di-phosphate: Prevents fall in pH.
